messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Stress: Stress, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was sixty-two when the accident happened, a bank teller at First Community Credit Union in suburban Cleveland for thirty-four years. He had always prided himself on steadiness—the kind of man colleagues relied on, the one who stayed late to balance the drawer, who mentored younger tellers without impatience. His wife, Susan, had often said he was unflappable. That was before.

It was a Tuesday afternoon in March when a delivery driver, hurrying to make his next stop, pushed through the staff door without knocking. Marcus was helping his nephew Derek, twenty-three, newly hired and still learning the cash-handling procedures. Derek had been struggling—nervous with customers, slow to count—and Marcus had volunteered to walk him through a particularly complex transaction involving a business account deposit. They were standing at the back counter, Marcus's hand on Derek's shoulder, guiding him through the ledger entry, when the driver burst through. Marcus turned instinctively, startled, and his arm swung outward. His elbow caught Derek's temple with a force neither of them had anticipated. Derek went down hard, his head striking the metal edge of the counter on the way. The sound—a crack that Marcus would later realize he could never quite unhear—echoed through the office.

Derek spent four days in the hospital with a severe concussion and a fractured skull. He recovered, eventually, though he never returned to the bank. But for Marcus, something fractured that did not mend.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found himself unable to settle. He would lie beside Susan at night, his body rigid, listening to every sound in the house—the furnace cycling, the neighbor's dog, the distant hum of traffic on the interstate. He had come to believe that vigilance was the only thing standing between him and another catastrophe, that if he relaxed for even a moment, if he allowed himself the luxury of true sleep, he would fail someone again. Sleep became impossible. He would lie awake until three or four in the morning, his mind cycling through the moment: the door opening, his arm moving, the sound. When he finally dozed, fragments of the scene would surface without warning—Derek's face, the angle of the counter, his own hand—and vanish just as suddenly, leaving him gasping.

At work, Marcus began to change. He moved carefully, deliberately, avoiding the staff area where the accident occurred. When a colleague approached from behind, even to ask a simple question, Marcus would startle violently, his heart racing. He found himself unable to relax even when he was alone in the break room, even when he knew intellectually that nothing bad was happening. His shoulders stayed high. His jaw clenched. Susan noticed that he flinched when she touched him unexpectedly—reaching for his arm to show him something, or brushing past him in the kitchen. The warmth that had characterized their marriage for thirty-eight years began to cool, replaced by a careful distance he maintained without meaning to.

He began to see himself differently. When he looked in the mirror, he saw a man who had caused serious harm, who had failed at the one thing he had always believed he was good at: being steady, being safe. The guilt that arose when he remembered the event was not a passing thought but a physical sensation, a weight in his chest that made breathing difficult. He was certain now that he had permanently changed for the worse, that whatever steadiness people had once seen in him had been an illusion, that his reactions to the accident—the sleeplessness, the hypervigilance, the way he had begun to withdraw from his family—proved he was simply a lousy coper, a man who fell apart when it mattered most.

By late fall, nearly eight months after the accident, Marcus could no longer hide what was happening. His supervisor had noticed his deterioration, his inability to focus, the way he had begun calling in sick more frequently. Susan, finally, insisted he see someone. He sat in the waiting room of the therapist's office, terrified and ashamed, uncertain whether anything could repair what he had broken—in Derek, in himself, in the life he thought he had been living.
